title: The House
subtitle: A man lives alone in an enormous building of endless halls, with the sea moving through the lower floors. He is calm, grateful and exact. How does a writer make a strange place feel like home?

card.who: Susanna Clarke · Piranesi · the world of the book
card.essence: A building with no outside, tides in the corridors and statues in every hall. How the narrator describes it, and how to describe a place so well that a listener can see it.

intention: you'll talk about the strange world of the book, use a four-step way of describing a place in precise detail, and practise the language of noticing, comparing and wondering.
warmup: Think of a place you know so well that you could describe it with your eyes closed. What would you mention first?
Have you ever been alone somewhere for a long time? What did you start to notice that you would normally miss?
If you could live in one enormous building for a year, what would you want it to contain?

vocab.heading: A · What do they mean here? Work it out from the context
vocab.intro: Read the sentence, guess the meaning of the word in bold, then reveal.

items.sent: The explorers got lost in the labyrinth of corridors and had to follow the sound of water to find their way out.
items.meaning: labyrinth (noun) — a complicated network of paths or passages in which it is easy to lose your way. A maze is similar. Adjective: labyrinthine.

items.sent: From the balcony they looked out over a vast hall that seemed to have no far wall.
items.meaning: vast (adjective) — extremely large in size or extent.

items.sent: He lived a solitary life and found that he did not mind it.
items.meaning: solitary (adjective) — alone, or done alone. Compare lonely, which means sad because you are alone; solitary can be neutral or even pleasant.

items.sent: Each morning he checked the water levels, a small ritual that organised the day.
items.meaning: ritual (noun) — a set of actions done regularly and in the same way, often with a sense of meaning.

vocab.heading: B · Which term means…?
vocab.intro: Three terms: take stock · keep track of · in awe of. Say the right one, then reveal.

items.sent: Which term means to stop and think carefully about a situation before deciding what to do next?
items.meaning: take stock — At the end of the year she took stock of what she had learned.

items.sent: Which term means to follow the progress or position of something so that you always know where it is?
items.meaning: keep track of — He wrote everything down so that he could keep track of the tides. Opposite: lose track of.

items.sent: Which term means feeling great respect and wonder, sometimes mixed with fear?
items.meaning: in awe of — They stood in awe of the size of the building. Noun: awe.

vocab.heading: C · Which word completes all three phrases?
vocab.intro: One missing word fits every phrase in the group. Say it, then reveal.

items.sent: keep a ___  ·  write in a ___  ·  an old ___
items.meaning: journal — a daily or regular written record of what you do, see or think.

items.sent: a rising ___  ·  a high ___  ·  the ___ goes out
items.meaning: tide — the regular rise and fall of the sea. Also: the tide turns, go against the tide.

items.sent: a marble ___  ·  a bronze ___  ·  carve a ___
items.meaning: statue — a figure of a person or animal made from stone, metal or another hard material.

vocab_use: When did you last take stock of your own life? What did you decide?
What do you do to keep track of things you do not want to forget?
What has left you in awe in the last year, a place, a person, a piece of work?

story.heading: Part 1 — A house the size of a world
paras: Susanna Clarke's novel Piranesi begins inside a building that seems to have no beginning and no end. There are halls opening into halls, each one lined with statues, each one different. Some are dry. In the lower halls the sea comes in, rises, fills the floor and goes out again. In the highest halls the clouds drift in and sometimes become rain.

The narrator knows no other place. As far as he is concerned, this is the world, and he calls it the House. He has explored a great deal of it, and he describes it with an extraordinary calm, naming the halls by their statues and measuring the distance between places in days of walking.
The first thing the reader notices is his voice. He is careful, grateful and curious. He treats the House as something kind that provides for him, and he never complains.
checks: What is the narrator's attitude to it?
answers: An enormous building of connected halls with statues in each one, tides in the lower halls and clouds in the upper ones.
Calm, grateful and curious. He sees it as kind and generous.
In days of walking, not in miles or minutes.
story.discuss: A narrator who has never known anything else describes the place as a gift. What does that tell you about how we see the world we grow up in?

story.heading: Part 2 — A life with a pattern
paras: His days have a shape. He watches the tides and knows the times when certain halls are dangerous. He catches fish and collects seaweed to eat. He sleeps in a hall away from the water, and he looks after the bones of the dead who lie in some of the niches, leaving them small offerings. He is quite sure that the dead are not gone from the House, only changed.
He also writes. He keeps journals and an index of them, so that he can find any entry again. Writing is how he makes sense of a place that is too large to see. It is a quiet, orderly kind of courage.

There is one other living person, a man he calls the Other, who visits him a couple of times a week. The Other is polite, a little impatient, and always in a hurry. He wants Piranesi's help in a search that he describes only in very general terms.
checks: How does he fill his days?
answers: He watches the tides, finds food, looks after the bones of the dead and writes.
To make sense of a place too large to see, and to find things again with the index.
The only other living person he knows, who visits regularly and wants his help.
story.discuss: The narrator's routine is calm and repetitive. What do you find attractive about a life with that much order, and what would you find hard?

story.heading: Part 3 — Why it feels strange
paras: The reader soon senses that something is wrong. The narrator never asks where the House came from or how he arrived in it. He accepts things that would puzzle most people, and he describes some of them very precisely and understands very little of what they imply.

This is the clever part of the book's design. We see the House through a person who loves it and who cannot see its edges. We are close to him and also slightly ahead of him, and the gap between what he says and what we begin to suspect is what drives the story.

People who love the novel often say that the writing is the main pleasure: the patient lists, the names, the sense of a mind paying attention. Others find it slow at the start. Both groups usually agree that the first chapters make a very particular mood.
checks: What does the narrator never ask?
How does the reader feel in relation to the narrator?
What do people usually say about the writing?
answers: Where the House came from, or how he got there.
Close to him, but slightly ahead, so we suspect things he does not.
That the style and the mood are the main pleasure, though some find it slow at first.
story.discuss: Do you enjoy a narrator who understands less than you do? Can you think of another book or film that works that way?

tool_tab.lead: A good description is not a list of facts. It is the result of looking slowly. The Slow Look is a loop of four moves you can use on any place: look without hurrying, name what you see exactly, compare it with something familiar, and wonder what the place says about the people who made or use it.
how: Look: stay with the place for a full minute before you speak. Notice what is large, what is small, what moves, what is still.
Name: choose precise words. Not a big room but a long hall with a stone floor and a statue in each niche.
Compare: link it with something your listener knows. It felt like an empty railway station at four in the morning.
Wonder: end with a question or an idea, not a fact. I kept wondering who had put all the statues there, and why.

sort.intro: Each sentence is part of a description of a place. Which move of the Slow Look is it?

items.text: For a long moment I did nothing but listen to the water.
items.why: it shows slow attention before any description.

items.text: A narrow stone staircase with eleven steps, each worn smooth in the middle.
items.why: it uses exact details, a number and a specific condition.

items.text: It reminded me of the corridors in my old school after everyone had gone home.
items.why: it links the place to a familiar memory.

items.text: I could not stop asking myself who would build a house so large.
items.why: it ends with a question about meaning, not a fact.

items.text: The light came in low and yellow through a gap in the roof.
items.why: it records what the eye notices: light, direction, colour.

items.text: A marble figure of a man holding a rope, about twice my height.
items.why: it gives the material, the pose and the scale.

items.text: It felt like standing inside a very large, very patient animal.
items.why: a surprising comparison that gives the feeling, not only the facts.

items.text: Perhaps the quiet was part of what the place was for.
items.why: it suggests an idea about purpose.

breaks: Too many details. Choose the three that matter. A description that lists everything shows nothing.
Borrowed comparisons. Like a movie or like a dream tell the listener nothing. Compare with something specific from your own life.
No wondering. A description with no question or idea at the end is only a list. Finish with what the place made you think.
discuss: Which move do you usually skip: looking slowly, naming exactly, comparing or wondering?
Describe a place from your childhood in three sentences using only Name and Compare. Then add a Wonder.

grammar.name: Describing a place precisely
grammar.lead: A precise description depends on a few structures that add detail without making the sentence heavy: prepositions of place, participle adjectives and short relative clauses.
notes: Prepositions and positions: a statue in a niche above the doorway, a pool at the foot of the stairs, a window high up in the wall, a corridor leading off to the left. Choose the preposition that shows exactly where.
Participle adjectives (-ed and -ing): a worn step, a broken column, a flooded hall, a rising tide, a sleeping bird. The -ed form says what has happened to it; the -ing form says what it is doing.
Short relative clauses: a hall where the water was always cold; a statue which seemed to be listening; the staircase that nobody used. Use where for places and which or that for things.

exercises.heading: Choose the form
exercises.intro: Put the verb in brackets into the correct participle form.
items: 2. A ___ (sleep) bird sat on the statue's shoulder.
3. The steps were ___ (wear) smooth by years of use.
4. They heard the ___ (rise) sound of water in the lower hall.
answers: 1. flooded — the corridor has been flooded (passive meaning)

exercises.heading: Join the details
exercises.intro: Combine each pair into one sentence with where, which or that.
items: 1. There was a hall. The tide never reached it.
2. He pointed to a statue. It held a long rope.
3. She described a staircase. Nobody used it.
4. They found a room. The walls were covered in writing.
answers: 1. There was a hall where the tide never reached. (or: a hall that the tide never reached)
2. He pointed to a statue which held a long rope.
3. She described a staircase that nobody used.
4. They found a room where the walls were covered in writing.

grammar.closing: Now describe a room you know well in four sentences. Include one participle adjective, one relative clause and two prepositions of place.

speak.intro: Choose a task, start the timer and talk. On your own it works as a talk; with a partner or a group, take turns and respond to each other.
speak.useful: “It felt like…” · “What struck me was…” · “There was a… which…” · “I kept wondering…” · “Above the door there was…”

tasks.label: Task 1 — The place in the book
paras: Describe the House to someone who has not read the book. Use the Slow Look: what you see, the exact details, a comparison and a question.

tasks.label: Task 2 — Your own place
paras: Describe somewhere that matters to you, a room, a street or a view. Take thirty seconds to look in your mind, then speak for a minute using all four moves.

tasks.label: Task 3 — The narrator's voice
paras: The narrator is calm, grateful and exact. Pick one thing in your day and describe it in that voice, as if it were the most important thing in the world.

final: The narrator loves a place that other people might find frightening. What decides whether we love or fear a strange place?
Is it a good thing to be as content as the narrator? What might he be missing?
Does a house shape the person who lives in it? Give an example from your own life.
From memory: describe the House in five sentences, using vast, keep track of and in awe of, and finish with a wondering.
